title: Sealed marriage endures beyond death, and plural marriage is justified by command
setting: On 12 July 1843, Joseph Smith dictated this revelation to William Clayton in his Nauvoo office. The official heading says Joseph likely knew some of its principles well before 1843. Hyrum Smith urged him to write it down, hoping it would persuade Emma Smith to accept plural marriage. The Joseph Smith Papers editors count about twenty-five confidential plural sealings by then, many unknown to Emma. Emma rejected the document and later destroyed the original, but a copy by Joseph Kingsbury survived. It was first published in 1852 and added to the Doctrine and Covenants in 1876.
summary: The revelation answers Joseph’s question about how God justified Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, David, and Solomon in having many wives and concubines. It reveals a “new and everlasting covenant,” saying covenants not sealed by the Holy Spirit of promise end at death. Marriages made only for this world end then, but marriages sealed by the one holding the keys endure toward exaltation. It says Abraham did not sin in taking Hagar and concubines because God commanded it, and David sinned only concerning Uriah’s wife. It confirms Joseph’s power to seal on earth and in heaven. Emma Smith is told to receive Joseph’s wives and cleave to him or be destroyed; if she forgives him, she will be blessed. Under the “law of the priesthood,” a man may marry more virgins with his first wife’s consent. If she rejects the law, verse 64 says she will be destroyed, and verse 65 frees him from “the law of Sarah,” her consent.

contextNote.title: What makes a covenant last
contextNote.text: Joseph asked about ancient plural marriages, but the revelation first sets a wider rule. Verse 7 says every covenant or contract ends at death unless it is sealed by the Holy Spirit of promise. It must also be made through the one person appointed to hold “this power,” named as Joseph. Verse 15 applies the rule to marriage: a covenant made “so long as he is in the world” ends with death. Verse 19 states the contrast, a sealed marriage “of full force when they are out of the world”. The later verses on plural marriage (verses 34–39 and 61–65) rest on this same claim of sealing authority. In this passage, “sealed” means authorized by God through a single key holder so that a bond outlasts death.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 129–132 draws eternal families from verses 13–21 and calls plural marriage acceptable only when God commands it. How do verses 1–2 and 29–40 present the revelation as an answer to Joseph’s question about ancient prophets?

newPeople.name: Abraham
newPeople.why: named in vv. 1, 29–37, 49–50, 57, 65; the biblical patriarch whose marriages and promises the revelation discusses

reviewNote: Read all 66 verses. Official heading gives Nauvoo, recorded 12 July 1843, with some principles likely known earlier, and refers readers to Official Declaration 1. JSP historical introduction read: dictated in Joseph’s office in the brick store, Clayton as scribe over about three hours; Hyrum’s request; Emma’s rejection and later destruction of the original; Joseph C. Kingsbury’s copy for Newel K. Whitney as the source of all later texts; first published 14 September 1852; D&C 1876. JSP says an early-1830s revelation rests on later recollections, not a located pre-1843 document. JSP also notes Emma had briefly accepted the practice in May 1843. The ‘about twenty-five’ count is the JSP editors’ figure; other historians give different totals, so it is attributed. Verse 51 (‘that which I commanded you to offer unto her’) is unclear in the record and is not interpreted. Isaac, Jacob, David, Solomon, Sarah, Hagar, Nathan, Uriah, and Aaron are named but not added as people; Abraham added as a newPerson because he is central. Fact-check 2026-10-12: summary’s last sentence (“if she rejects it, he is exempt”) was vague and left out verse 64’s warning to a wife who rejects the law. Rewritten to state verses 61–65 accurately.
